items.label: Research question
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the INTRODUCTION that sets up what the study wants to find out (just before the hypothesis).
items.model: Does training in expressive writing of positive emotions change test anxiety in senior-high-school students?
items.why: 'It would be interesting to determine whether…' is the research question in disguise; the hypothesis follows immediately.

items.label: Hypothesis
items.prompt: Find the hypothesis.
items.model: Expressive writing of positive emotion would reduce senior-high-school students' test anxiety.
items.why: 'We therefore hypothesized…' states the hypothesis.

items.label: Independent variable
items.prompt: What is the independent variable? Name both groups.
items.model: Type of writing: expressive writing of positive emotions (EW) vs writing about daily activities (CW).
items.why: The IV is what differed between the randomly assigned groups.

items.label: Dependent variable
items.prompt: What is the main dependent variable?
items.model: Post-test test anxiety (TAS score).
items.why: The ANCOVA section states the DV directly: post-test TAS scores.

items.label: Conceptual definition (test anxiety)
items.prompt: Find the conceptual definition of TEST ANXIETY.
items.model: A form of academic stress characterised by nervousness before or during an exam.
items.why: The first sentence of the Introduction defines the key outcome.

items.label: Conceptual definition (expressive writing)
items.prompt: Find the conceptual definition of EXPRESSIVE WRITING.
items.model: Writing a deep, meaningful piece about a personally significant topic.
items.why: '…refers to…' signals the definition. It appears in the middle of the Introduction, not at the start.

items.label: Operational definition
items.prompt: How was test anxiety measured? Find the sentence describing the items and scoring.
items.model: Sarason's Test Anxiety Scale: 37 yes/no items (yes = 1); 20+ = severe anxiety.
items.why: The Measures subsection names the scale and explains its scoring.

items.label: Research gap
items.prompt: Find the sentence pointing out a weakness of earlier expressive-writing interventions.
items.model: Most earlier interventions were carried out just before exams or in a lab, which may be too short for chronic anxiety.
items.why: 'However, most of the interventions were…' signals the gap. It explains why they chose a 30-day intervention.

items.label: Cultural rationale
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining why POSITIVE (not negative) emotional writing suits Chinese students.
items.model: Writing positive emotions is more in accordance with Chinese culture, which tends to suppress negative emotions.
items.why: Part of the justification for the study is cultural; 'Hence' signals the conclusion of that argument.

items.label: General method
items.prompt: What general method did this study use?
items.model: RCT: students were randomly assigned (odd/even random numbers) to EW or CW.
items.why: Random assignment plus a control group = randomised controlled trial.

items.label: Sample
items.prompt: Find the sentence describing the 75 participants who were recruited for the experiment.
items.model: 75 students with severe test anxiety (21 male, 54 female, mean age 16.84).
items.why: 200 were screened, 185 gave valid responses, and 75 with severe anxiety entered the experiment. Read carefully.

items.label: Random assignment
items.prompt: Find the sentence describing HOW students were assigned to groups.
items.model: By random computer numbers: odd numbers to EW, even numbers to CW.
items.why: Random assignment is what makes this an experiment.

items.label: Group equivalence check
items.prompt: Find the sentence showing the two groups were similar BEFORE the intervention.
items.model: No significant difference in pre-test TAS between groups, F(1, 73) = 0.62, p > .05.
items.why: Checking baseline equivalence confirms random assignment worked.

items.label: Manipulation
items.prompt: Find the sentence describing what the EXPERIMENTAL group did.
items.model: Wrote about positive emotions felt each day, 20 minutes a day for 30 days.
items.why: The control group's task is described two sentences later.

items.label: Was the hypothesis supported?
items.prompt: Was the hypothesis supported?
items.model: Supported: EW post-test TAS was significantly lower than CW (F = 135.80, p < .001; effect size 2.02).
items.why: The group effect was significant and in the predicted direction.

items.label: Gender
items.prompt: Did the effect of the intervention differ between males and females?
options: Yes, it worked better for female students
Yes, it worked better for male students
items.model: No: the group × gender interaction was non-significant (F = 0.09).
items.why: An interaction tests whether the effect of one variable depends on another; here it didn't.

items.label: Explanation (mechanism)
items.prompt: In the Discussion, find the sentence proposing the psychological PROCESS through which writing may reduce anxiety.
items.model: Students may have undergone cognitive reappraisal of test anxiety through emotional expression.
items.why: The mechanism (cognitive reappraisal and self-regulation) is only proposed in the Discussion, hedged with 'could have'.

items.label: Practical implication
items.prompt: Find the sentence recommending the method for SCHOOLS.
items.model: It can be used with many students at once, so it is worth promoting in schools.
items.why: Practical implications describe real-world use.

items.label: Limitations
items.prompt: Find the limitation about what the study did NOT measure.
items.model: Only test anxiety was measured, not changes in exam performance.
items.why: Three limitations are given (generalisability, no performance measure, long intervention). This prompt asks for the measurement one.

items.label: Limitation (generalisability)
items.prompt: Find the limitation about GENERALISABILITY.
items.model: Students were recruited only from Xinxiang City.
items.why: Generalisability = whether results apply beyond this sample.
